the neural bases of experimentally engended self-esteem are found in medial prefrontal and temporopariatal cortices.

the neural correlates of self-esteem, and how these are influenced by self-referential processes.
the neural correlates of self-esteem.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the neural correlates of self-esteem are complex, and that self-esteem is a multidimensional construct that may not be adequately captured by a single fMRI paradigm.
there are a number of neural correlates of self-esteem.

self-esteem is a multidimensional concept that is not easily captured with a single measure, and that the brain regions that are activated during the self-referential process may vary as a function of the specific task used to elicit self-referential thoughts.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

individual differences in self-esteem are mediated by a distributed network of neural regions that include the medial prefrontals, the temporoparietal regions, the anterior and posterior cingulate, and the precuneus.

self-esteem is an affective, evaluative, social construct that is mediated by a distributed network of brain regions, including the medial prefrontl cortex, anterior and posterior cingulate cortex, precuneus and left temporoparital cortex, and that individual differences in self-esteem are associated with individual differences in affective, evaluational, and social cognitive processes, and in the neural substrates mediating them.

self-esteem is not just a matter of self-evaluative processes but also a matter of social cognitive and affect processing, which may be differentially engaged by positive and negative self-referential stimuli.
The main takeaway from our work is that
self-esteem is not simply a function of the self-referential network, but rather the self-referent network is a critical component of the self-esteem network.
the neural bases of self-esteem are likely to be highly variable across individuals and may not be as stable as previously thought.
self-esteem is not a static trait, but a complex, dynamic construct that is mediated by the brain.
